questions.q: Which security goal does a denial-of-service attack primarily target?
choices: Confidentiality
Integrity
Availability
Non-repudiation
questions.explain: A DoS attack tries to make a machine or piece of software unavailable, so that it cannot perform its basic function.

questions.q: To take a system down, a DoS attacker must exhaust every one of the system's resources.
questions.explain: Different parts of a system have different resource limits. The attacker only needs to exhaust the part with the least resources, the bottleneck.

questions.q: Why do DoS attackers so often spoof the source IP address?
choices: Spoofed packets get higher priority from routers, so they reach the target faster
The attacker doesn't need replies, and using a fresh fake source address for each packet hides the attacker and defeats IP blacklisting
The target's TCP stack only accepts packets from addresses it has already seen
Spoofing lets the attacker read the server's responses without being detected
questions.explain: A DoS attacker doesn't care about responses. A unique spoofed source on every packet hides the attacker's identity and stops the target from identifying and blocking a single address.

questions.q: Why is a DoS attack launched from a single machine usually impractical today?
choices: ISPs block any host that sends more than a fixed number of packets per second
TCP no longer allows a single host to open more than one connection to a server
Modern servers can handle far more bandwidth than one machine can generate
IP spoofing cannot be done from a single machine
questions.explain: Modern server bandwidth is much larger than what one machine can send. That is why attackers turn to many machines at once (DDoS).

questions.q: What is the term for a large network of compromised, remotely controllable machines that attackers often use to carry out DDoS attacks?
questions.explain: Botnets let an attacker point traffic from thousands of compromised machines at a single target.

questions.q: With good enough traffic filtering, a server can completely eliminate the possibility of a DDoS attack.
questions.explain: The bandwidth a server can provide is always limited, so DDoS can only be mitigated, never fully eliminated.

questions.q: Some DDoS protections analyze incoming traffic and drop packets from sources that use too much bandwidth. What makes this defense especially difficult?
choices: Encryption hides how large each packet is
IP spoofing hides the bots' identities and gives inconsistent information about where the traffic comes from
Bots always use TCP, and TCP traffic cannot be rate-limited
Routers strip source addresses before packets reach the server
questions.explain: Per-source limits depend on knowing the real source. Spoofed addresses make the traffic look like it comes from many unrelated places.

questions.q: Many application-level DoS attacks rely on asymmetry. What does asymmetry mean here?
choices: The attacker uses more upload bandwidth than the server uses for downloads
The attacker and the server use different encryption keys
Only the server, not the attacker, has to complete the TCP handshake
A small amount of input from the attacker causes a large amount of resource consumption
questions.explain: Asymmetric attacks get a lot of leverage: cheap requests from the attacker make the application spend a large amount of resources.

questions.q: Which of these are application-level resource-exhaustion attacks?
choices: Repeatedly calling write to fill up filesystem space
Repeatedly calling malloc to exhaust RAM
Eavesdropping on traffic to steal session cookies
Repeatedly calling fork to use up processing threads
Issuing operations that saturate disk I/O
Modifying a packet's payload in transit
questions.explain: Filesystem space, RAM, threads and disk I/O are all application resources that can be exhausted. Eavesdropping and tampering attack confidentiality and integrity, not availability.

questions.q: What are the three prongs of the usual defense against application-level DoS?
choices: Encryption, authentication, integrity
Identification, isolation, quotas
Detection, response, recovery
Overprovisioning, filtering, spoofing
questions.explain: Identify (tell users apart), isolate (one user can't affect another), and apply quotas (cap each user's share of resources).

questions.q: Which prong of the application-level DoS defense ensures that one user's actions do not affect another user's experience?
choices: Identification
Quotas
Isolation
Proof-of-work
questions.explain: Isolation keeps users' resource use separate so that one user cannot degrade service for others.

questions.q: A hosting service limits each user to 4 GB of RAM and 2 CPU cores. Which DoS defense is this?
choices: Identification
Overprovisioning
SYN cookies
Quotas
questions.explain: Placing a fixed limit on each user is a quota. It ensures every user can only use a certain share of resources.

questions.q: How does requiring proof-of-work (such as a CAPTCHA) help against DoS?
choices: It makes each request cost the requester resources, so flooding becomes more expensive for the attacker
It encrypts requests so the attacker cannot replay them
It reveals the attacker's true IP address to the server
It reduces the server's cost of handling each request to zero
questions.explain: Proof-of-work forces users to spend resources before they can issue a request. That raises the attacker's cost of sending many requests.

questions.q: The identification step, which distinguishes and authenticates users, can itself be expensive and become a target for DoS.
questions.explain: Authenticating every requester costs resources, so the identification process can be vulnerable to DoS too.

questions.q: What does an attacker do in a SYN flood?
choices: Completes many TCP handshakes, then sends huge amounts of data on each connection
Sends many ACK packets with no SYN before them
Sends many SYN packets, ignores the SYN/ACK replies, and never sends the final ACK
Replays a legitimate client's SYN/ACK to hijack its connection
questions.explain: The attacker starts many handshakes and never finishes them, leaving the server waiting on many half-open connections.

questions.q: Which server resource does a SYN flood exhaust?
choices: Memory holding per-connection state (such as sequence numbers) for handshakes that never complete
Disk space used to log rejected packets
CPU time spent decrypting TLS sessions
The server's pool of available IP addresses
questions.explain: The server has to remember sequence numbers to match each expected ACK. With no ACKs arriving, that memory fills up and blocks legitimate connections.

questions.q: In a SYN flood with spoofed source addresses, where do the server's SYN/ACK replies go?
choices: Back to the attacker's real address
To the spoofed, essentially random addresses, not to the attacker
Nowhere, because the server drops spoofed SYNs before replying
To the server's default gateway, which discards them
questions.explain: The server replies to whatever source address the SYN claims. With spoofing, that address is random and is not the attacker's.

questions.q: With SYN cookies, where is the connection state kept between sending the SYN/ACK and receiving the client's ACK?
choices: In a server-side table indexed by the client's IP address
In an HTTP cookie stored by the client's browser
In a special TCP option that every client is required to store
Encoded with a server secret in the SYN/ACK's sequence number, which the client echoes back in its ACK number
questions.explain: TCP has no field meant for storing state, so the server packs the state, protected by a secret, into its sequence number. The client hands it back in the ACK number.

questions.q: With SYN cookies, the server allocates connection state as soon as it receives a SYN.
questions.explain: The server allocates state only after the handshake completes and the cookie in the ACK checks out against the secret.

questions.q: Why can't an attacker who spoofs source addresses make a SYN-cookie server allocate connection state?
choices: The SYN/ACK carrying the cookie goes to the spoofed address, so the attacker never sees it and cannot return a valid cookie in an ACK
SYN-cookie servers reject all packets with a source port above 1024
SYN cookies encrypt the entire TCP connection
The server pings each source address to confirm it before replying
questions.explain: State is created only when an ACK returns a valid cookie. A spoofing attacker never receives the cookie and cannot forge one without the secret, so it never completes the handshake.

questions.q: Why is overprovisioning (giving the server a lot of memory) considered a weak defense against SYN floods?
choices: It makes the server more vulnerable to IP spoofing
It breaks the TCP handshake for legitimate clients
It is expensive, and a strong enough attacker can still exhaust the extra memory
Extra memory makes the server slower to respond
questions.explain: More memory only raises the bar. It costs money, and depending on the threat model an attacker can still fill it.

questions.q: In the SYN-cookie defense, which TCP header field of the SYN/ACK carries the encoded state?
questions.explain: The server encodes the state, with a secret, in the sequence number. The client returns it in the ACK number.

questions.q: What principle is behind the hardening advice 'turn off every unnecessary network service'?
choices: Unused services use bandwidth that an attacker could exploit for DoS
Bugs in code you don't run can't hurt you, so less functionality means fewer chances for vulnerabilities
Fewer services make encryption keys harder to guess
Disabled services automatically act as honeypots
questions.explain: Every network service you run might contain an exploitable bug. Code you don't run can't hurt you.

questions.q: Why does hardening each machine individually become infeasible for an organization with thousands of computers?
choices: Hardening tools can only run on one machine per network
Disabling services on many machines at once causes a DoS
Firewalls stop working once too many machines are hardened
Machines differ in OS, hardware and user needs, even listing them all is hard, and one missed machine can become a launching point for attacks
questions.explain: At large scale, the variety of machines and needs, plus the risk of missing even one machine, make per-machine hardening impractical. This motivates blocking access in the network instead.

questions.q: Under an outbound-only policy, which of these connections is allowed?
choices: An external customer connecting to the company's public web server
An external mail server delivering email to the company's mail server
An employee's internal machine connecting to an external news website
A remote user connecting to an internal FTP server
questions.explain: Outbound-only allows every connection initiated by an internal user and denies every inbound connection. The other three options are all inbound.

questions.q: What is the main problem with an outbound-only policy for a large organization?
choices: It is too restrictive: the organization cannot run any publicly reachable service, such as a web or mail server
It lets external users reach every internal service
It fails open whenever a rule is missing
It requires inspecting the content of every outbound connection
questions.explain: Because no internal service is visible from outside, public web, mail and FTP servers become impossible. That is why policies need more flexibility.

questions.q: An inbound connection is one initiated by an internal user to contact an external service.
questions.explain: That describes an outbound connection. An inbound connection is initiated by an external user trying to reach a service on an internal machine.

questions.q: In the firewall's access control policy, each network service on each internal machine is an object. If a company has 40 internal machines and each runs 5 network services, how many objects are there?
questions.explain: Objects are the set of network services on all inside machines: 40 x 5 = 200.

questions.q: Which statement correctly pairs each default policy with how it fails?
choices: Default-deny (whitelist) fails open; default-allow (blacklist) fails closed
Default-deny (whitelist) fails closed; default-allow (blacklist) fails open
Default-deny (blacklist) fails closed; default-allow (whitelist) fails open
Both fail closed, because unknown traffic is always dropped
questions.explain: Default-deny lists only allowed services, so a mistake blocks something (fails closed). Default-allow lists only denied services, so a mistake exposes something (fails open).

questions.q: An administrator using a default-allow policy forgets to put a newly vulnerable service on the deny list. What is the likely result?
choices: Users quickly complain that the service is unreachable
The firewall automatically drops that service's traffic
Nothing, because default-allow only applies to outbound traffic
A security breach that may go unnoticed for a long time
questions.explain: Default-allow fails open. The vulnerable service stays exposed, and attackers who break in are unlikely to announce it.

questions.q: An administrator using a default-deny policy forgets to add a safe, needed service to the allow list. What is the likely result?
choices: Loss of functionality, which users notice and report, so it is easy to fix
A hidden security breach
The firewall switches to default-allow for that service
External attackers gain access to the forgotten service
questions.explain: Default-deny fails closed. The cost is lost availability, not a breach, and the omission becomes obvious right away.

questions.q: How does a firewall policy identify a single network service?
choices: (hostname, username, password)
(MAC address, IP address, port number)
(IP address, protocol TCP or UDP, port number)
(port number, application name, OS version)
questions.explain: A service is the triplet (m, r, p): machine IP address, protocol identifier and port. For example, (1.2.3.4, TCP, 80) is a web server.

questions.q: Why is default-allow described as a losing arms race?
choices: It requires buying a new firewall whenever a threat appears
Defenders must keep up with and stay ahead of every new attack, but attackers outnumber them and only need to win once
It forces users to request access for every new service
It blocks so much traffic that attackers switch to DDoS
questions.explain: With a deny list, every new threat has to be found and added in time. Attackers are more numerous and need only one success.

questions.q: Why is a firewall placed at a choke point in the network?
choices: Choke points have the highest bandwidth in the network
Choke points are the only place where packets are unencrypted
It gives one place where all traffic can be monitored and a policy enforced for thousands of machines
Choke points automatically block spoofed source addresses
questions.explain: Like an airport security checkpoint, a choke point lets you check everything in one place instead of at thousands of entrances.

questions.q: A packet filter's policy is an ordered list of rules. How is a packet's handling decided?
choices: The last matching rule decides
The first matching rule decides
The most specific matching rule decides, regardless of order
The majority of matching rules decides
questions.explain: The firewall checks the rules one by one, and the first rule that matches decides whether the packet is allowed or dropped.

questions.q:
A firewall has these rules, in order (initiator -> recipient):
1. allow tcp *:* -> 1.2.3.4:25
2. drop * *:* -> *:*
Which connection is allowed?
choices: An external host sending UDP to 1.2.3.4 port 25
An external host opening a TCP connection to 1.2.3.4 port 80
An external host opening a TCP connection to 1.2.3.5 port 25
An external host opening a TCP connection to 1.2.3.4 port 25
questions.explain: Only TCP connections to 1.2.3.4:25 match rule 1. Anything else (wrong protocol, port or machine) falls through to the drop-all rule.

questions.q:
Suppose the two rules are swapped so the order is:
1. drop * *:* -> *:*
2. allow tcp *:* -> 1.2.3.4:25
What happens to a TCP connection to 1.2.3.4 port 25?
choices: It is dropped, because the drop-all rule matches first
It is allowed, because the allow rule is more specific
It is allowed, because allow rules always override drop rules
It is dropped only if it comes from outside the network
questions.explain: First match wins, and the drop-all rule matches every packet, so rule 2 is never reached.

questions.q: Why does a stateful packet filter keep track of open connections?
choices: To encrypt traffic on established connections
To resend packets that were dropped
A packet from X to Y alone doesn't show whether X or Y started the connection; state shows whether it belongs to a connection that is already open
To count bytes so each user can be billed
questions.explain: Whether a packet should be forwarded can depend on who initiated the connection. State lets the filter recognize packets that belong to already-established connections.

questions.q: What must designers of a stateful packet filter be careful about?
choices: Storing the full contents of every packet for later inspection
Keeping only a small amount of information per connection so the firewall doesn't run out of memory
Never checking more than one rule per packet
Making sure the filter has no rules that mention UDP
questions.explain: Per-connection state uses memory. If that state is large, the firewall itself can be exhausted, which is the same weakness a SYN flood exploits on servers.

questions.q: Which kind of firewall could NOT enforce a policy that blocks FTP logins using the username 'root'?
choices: A stateful packet filter
An application-layer firewall
An FTP application proxy
A stateless packet filter that only looks at TCP, UDP and IP headers
questions.explain: The username is in the application data, not the headers. A stateless filter handles each packet by its headers alone with no memory, so it cannot follow the login.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of routing all web access through a web proxy (an application proxy)?
choices: The proxy has all the application-layer information about each request and reply, so it can make fine-grained allow/deny decisions
It removes the need for any security policy
It speeds up web traffic by bypassing the choke point
It does not need to understand the application protocol
questions.explain: Because the proxy takes part in the exchange itself, its monitoring can use everything about the request and reply when deciding.

questions.q: Which are drawbacks of application proxies (gateway proxies)?
choices: Implementation complexity: the proxy must understand every detail of the protocol it mediates
They can only see IP and TCP headers
Performance: funneling all of a site's traffic through a few proxies can overwhelm them
They cannot make allow/deny decisions
questions.explain: Proxies see the full application data and do make decisions. Their costs are protocol complexity and the risk of becoming a performance bottleneck.

questions.q: Application-layer firewalls can transform data on the fly instead of just allowing or dropping it.
questions.explain: Because they work on the content of data fields, application-layer firewalls can enforce stricter policies and modify data as it passes through.

questions.q: Which are the three properties every reference monitor should have?
choices: Unbypassable (always invoked)
Fail-open
Tamper-resistant
Stateful
Verifiable
Default-allow
questions.explain: A reference monitor must mediate every controlled operation, be protected from modification, and be simple enough for its correctness to be checked.

questions.q: An employee plugs an unsecured wireless access point into their internal machine, so anyone nearby can reach the internal network. Which reference-monitor property does this break?
choices: Tamper-resistant
Verifiable
Always invoked (unbypassable)
Orthogonal security
questions.explain: Traffic through the access point never crosses the firewall's choke point, so the firewall is bypassed. Complete mediation is lost.

questions.q: The set of all links between the internal network and the external world, every one of which a firewall must cover, is called the ___.
questions.explain: If any link in the security perimeter is left uncovered, the firewall can be bypassed.

questions.q: Why should a reference monitor be kept extremely simple?
choices: So it uses less bandwidth
So it can be verified, since checking the correctness of complex subsystems is generally beyond the state of the art
So attackers can't find it on the network
So it can run a standard operating system
questions.explain: Verifiability needs simplicity. Proving that a complex system correctly enforces a policy is generally not possible today.

questions.q: Which reference-monitor property do real-world firewalls generally fall short on most, and why?
choices: Always invoked, because firewalls cannot be placed at a choke point
Tamper-resistant, because firewalls must run many network services
None, because all three properties are routinely proven for firewalls
Verifiable, because firewall software and rule sets are too complex to verify systematically
questions.explain: Firewall correctness is generally not verified in practice. Bugs have let attackers send unexpected packets that defeat the policy, and rule sets quickly become complex.

questions.q: Which measures help make a firewall tamper-resistant?
choices: Not running a standard OS, user-level programs or network services on it
Allowing management access only from specific trusted machines
Making its rule set as long and detailed as possible
Ensuring the physical security of the firewall device
Letting any internal machine change its configuration
Protecting the firewall itself with firewall rules
questions.explain: Hardening means removing attack avenues, restricting who can manage the device, and guarding it physically. Longer rules don't stop tampering, and open configuration access invites it.

questions.q: What does it mean that firewalls provide orthogonal security?
choices: They can protect existing legacy systems without being built into them, and other components don't need to know the firewall is there
They protect confidentiality, integrity and availability independently
Every internal machine must be modified to cooperate with the firewall
They operate independently of any security policy
questions.explain: A filter that drops disallowed requests and passes allowed ones unchanged is transparent to the rest of the system, so it is easy to add to existing systems.

questions.q: Even if a firewall's code is completely correct, its rules may not enforce the access controls the operator believes they enforce.
questions.explain: Firewall policies quickly become complex. Correct code can still faithfully enforce the wrong rules.

questions.q: A new threat against an Internet service is discovered. Which firewall advantage lets an organization block it quickly for every internal machine?
choices: Central control
Orthogonal security
Stateless processing
Fail-open behavior
questions.explain: Only the firewall's policy has to change, not each machine, and every internal machine benefits immediately.

questions.q: Two users, each behind their own firewall, try to connect directly to each other peer-to-peer. Why does this usually fail?
choices: Firewalls block all outbound connections by default
P2P protocols cannot run over TCP
The receiving user's firewall sees the attempt as an inbound connection and blocks it
Both firewalls drop all traffic on port 80
questions.explain: This is the loss-of-functionality cost. Firewalls reduce connectivity from outside, and a peer's connection looks like any other inbound connection.

questions.q: Bill Cheswick described firewalled networks as 'a crunchy outer coating, with a soft, chewy center.' What does this capture?
choices: Firewalls stop insiders well but are weak against outsiders
Once an attacker gets inside the perimeter, they are trusted and can freely attack other inside machines
Firewalls are hard to configure but easy to bypass from outside
Internal machines are usually hardened better than the firewall
questions.explain: The perimeter is hard, but insiders are trusted. Once a bad actor is inside, the firewall can do nothing to stop attacks between inside machines.

questions.q: An employee's laptop picks up malware on hotel Wi-Fi with no firewall, then infects other machines after being plugged into the company network. Which firewall disadvantage does this show?
choices: Loss of functionality
Adversarial applications tunneling over port 80
Lack of central control
The malicious insider problem: anything inside the perimeter is trusted
questions.explain: The infected laptop is now an inside machine, and inside machines have unlimited power to attack each other.

questions.q: Why does an application tunneling its traffic over HTTP (port 80) make firewalls less effective?
choices: Many firewalls allow port 80, and they can't tell this traffic apart from real web traffic, so they lose visibility
Port 80 traffic is always encrypted
HTTP traffic skips the network's choke point
Firewalls then have to block all port 80 traffic, which breaks the web
questions.explain: To get past firewalls, developers hide their protocols inside allowed traffic. Over time, more traffic flows over port 80 and firewalls see less of what is really crossing them.

questions.q: Firewalls are easy to deploy, partly because they are essentially transparent to internal hosts.
questions.explain: Transparency gives an easy migration path, so firewalls can be deployed incrementally or all at once, and one firewall can protect thousands of machines.

questions.q: Firewalls are generally a much cheaper response to vulnerable network services than improving the quality of the code in all those services.
questions.explain: Cleaning up every service's code would be better in principle, but it is an enormous challenge. Firewalls address the problem far more cheaply.
